title: Succinct entangled proofs with efficient provers
formal: Does quantum circuit acceptance admit a uniform two-prover, one-round proof with a classical polynomial-time verifier, total classical communication \(O((\log(N+2))^k)\) for some fixed \(k\), completeness at least \(2/3\), and soundness at most \(1/3\) against arbitrary entangled provers, such that the honest provers can prepare and execute their strategy in quantum polynomial time given polynomially many copies of an accepting witness? Here \(N\) is the explicit circuit-instance length, and the instance, efficiency and soundness requirements are defined below.

source_formulation.text: The best of both worlds The essential reason that two-prover succinct verification remains an open problem is that nonlocal answer reduction is hard.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 3

why: This asks whether a classical verifier can check general quantumly provable claims using very little communication while keeping the honest quantum resources polynomial. It joins three substantial demands—two separated provers, unconditional soundness and succinct communication—and would clarify the practical content of entangled proof systems beyond their unconstrained complexity-class power.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The 2024 primary sources explicitly retain this efficient-honest-prover target. Checked 2025 and 2026 results improve general MIP* zero knowledge or computational QMA arguments, without supplying this conjunction of requirements. No matching resolution was found in the bounded search, and the cited proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: The source identifies the simultaneous two-prover succinctness and honest-efficiency requirement as open, while constructing a single-prover argument under cryptographic assumptions.
Fu–Mastel–Zhang give succinct perfect-zero-knowledge entangled proofs for recursively enumerable languages without the honest witness-efficiency guarantee required here.
Bartusek–Liu–Malavolta broaden the assumptions for succinct classical-verifier QMA arguments. The guarantee remains computational rather than unconditional.

importance.reason: A broad quantum verification question for a canonical QMA-complete promise problem, joining information-theoretic soundness, two-prover separation, short communication and polynomial honest resources. The tension between succinctness and witness-dependent prover efficiency connects quantum complexity with feasible verification, beyond a single protocol’s parameter optimization.

sentences: The question asks a classical verifier to check a quantum circuit’s acceptance using two separated quantum provers.
Both the questions and answers together must use only polylogarithmically many bits in the circuit description length.
Honest provers must prepare and execute their shared strategy efficiently from polynomially many copies of a valid quantum witness.
Cheating provers may use arbitrary finite-dimensional entanglement and unlimited computation, but cannot communicate while answering.
Known succinct computational arguments and entangled proofs without efficient honest preparation do not supply all of these requirements.

definitions: An instance is an explicitly listed quantum circuit \(U\) with \(w\) witness qubits, \(a\) auxiliary qubits initially in \(|0\rangle^{\otimes a}\), and a designated output qubit. The wire counts are included in unary and each gate and its wire indices are explicitly encoded in binary, so the total bit length \(N\) bounds the numbers of gates and wires. Use the fixed universal gate set \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\), where \(H|b\rangle=(|0\rangle+(-1)^b|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\mathbin\oplus c\rangle\), for bits \(b,c\). Acceptance means measuring output one in the computational basis. A YES instance has a normalized witness \(|\psi\rangle\) for which acceptance is at least \(2/3\); a NO instance has acceptance at most \(1/3\) for every witness density matrix, meaning every positive semidefinite trace-one matrix on the witness register. The input is promised to satisfy one of these cases. All parties know the circuit. The verifier uses private independent random bits, sends one classical question to each of two separated provers, receives one classical answer from each, and accepts or rejects in worst-case polynomial time in \(N\). Each prover sees only its own question. The worst-case sum of both question lengths and both answer lengths is at most \(C(\log_2(N+2))^k\), for constants \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge1\) independent of the instance and strategy. The verifier rejects overlong messages, and no uncharged timing or message-length channel is permitted. For completeness there must be fixed uniform quantum algorithms for setup and for each prover, and a fixed polynomial \(p\). For every YES instance some accepting witness \(|\psi\rangle\) enables the setup algorithm, given at most \(p(N)\) independent copies of \(|\psi\rangle\) and clean auxiliary qubits, to prepare the provers’ joint state using at most \(p(N)\) gates and qubits. Setup occurs before the verifier samples its questions and distributes the two shares of this state. Each local response then takes at most \(p(N)\) gates, qubits and classical computation steps. Uniform means that circuit descriptions and classical control are generated from the public instance and available local messages by fixed polynomial-time algorithms; arbitrary input-dependent advice is not supplied in addition to the witness copies. These algorithms may use the stated universal gates, computational-basis measurements and classical randomness and control. The resulting acceptance probability must be at least \(2/3\). For soundness, on every NO instance, acceptance must be at most \(1/3\) for every finite-dimensional shared state and every pair of local quantum measurement strategies, regardless of dimension or computational cost. In particular, a cheating strategy need not obey the honest resource bound. Its initial entanglement may depend on the instance but not on the verifier’s private questions. Neither honest nor cheating provers communicate after setup. All probabilities include the verifier’s randomness and measurement outcomes. This is an information-theoretically sound proof; no computational hardness assumption or security parameter is part of the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a verifier and uniform honest algorithms exist with some universal constants and polynomial bounds, or prove that no such protocol exists for the stated circuit promise problem. A positive answer must establish both efficient witness-dependent setup and local execution as well as soundness against unrestricted entangled cheating. Short questions with polynomial-length answers, a protocol with more than two provers or more rounds, an inefficient honest strategy, or a single-prover computational argument does not meet this particular target. The negation rules out every choice of the verifier, honest algorithms and fixed bounds; a limitation of one construction alone is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The circuit asks whether some quantum witness makes a known computation accept. The verifier sees the circuit description but receives only a very short classical exchange with two quantum devices. The witness itself need not have an efficiently computable classical description.

Entangled provers may share a joint quantum state before the test, even though they cannot exchange information while answering. Soundness must hold for every such cheating strategy. This is a stronger security demand than an argument whose guarantee assumes that cheating computations are efficient.

The honest side has a different resource requirement. Copies of a valid witness are allowed as input, but a vast precomputed state or an exponential computation hidden in setup is not. Natarajan and Nirkhe explicitly distinguish efficient setup from efficient responses, and explain why membership in a larger complexity class does not supply a witness-preserving efficient strategy.

Metger, Natarajan and Zhang identify succinct two-prover verification with efficient honest provers as unresolved. Their discussion distinguishes protocols with short questions from those with short total communication and distinguishes efficient honest strategies from general entangled proofs.

This card fixes the one-round nonlocal-game interpretation and ordinary polynomial verifier time. It expresses the quantum claim as an explicit circuit-acceptance promise problem and requires preparation from copies of an accepting circuit witness. It asks only for polylogarithmic total communication; it does not add the sharper logarithmic-question, constant-answer target of a quantum games PCP.

Fu, Mastel and Zhang’s 2025 paper gives two-prover, one-round succinct perfect-zero-knowledge proofs for every recursively enumerable language, a class that includes undecidable problems. Its main theorem does not supply polynomial-time honest preparation from QMA witness copies. An efficient simulator for zero knowledge is also not a pair of separated efficient provers.

Bartusek, Liu and Malavolta’s 2026 result broadens the assumptions under which succinct classical-verifier arguments for QMA exist: it assumes oblivious state preparation and collapsing hash functions. It remains a computational argument system. Its small communication therefore does not establish the unconditional two-prover proof requested here.
